newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia dam glitch puts focus on tycoon.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia dam glitch puts focus on tycoon.

text.p: Malaysia's $5.5 billion Bakun hydro-electric dam has stalled once again, throwing a spotlight on Ting Pek Khiing, the timber tycoon viewed as the linchpin in the controversial project.

Against considerable odds -- environmental challenges, viability and cost -- Ting has managed to steer the mammoth project up to the point of construction and the floating of the dam company's shares on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange.
So it is no wonder that Ting's Ekran Bhd stock dropped sharply after rumours emerged on Friday that the contract signing had been postponed because he was ill.
Ekran's stock fell to a low of 10.30 ringgit ($4.12) on Monday and was trading down 20 cents to 10.80 ringgit in late afternoon. Other Ting-affiliated companies also fell.

The pact was to be signed between Ekran and a consortium led by Asea Brown Boveri AG and Companhia Brasileria Projector e Obras (CBPO) on September 30 but was unexpectedly postponed for the second time this month.

Energy, Post and Telecommunications Minister Leo Moggie was quoted by the national news agency Bernama as saying on Monday that the postponement was because "the legal people and the contractors want to finalise the wordings of the agreement".
But talk about the gregarious, 50-something Ting's health has tantalised the market.

Ekran officials did not return repeated phone calls from Reuters, but sources at Singapore's Mount Elizabeth Hospital confirmed Ting was discharged on September 28 after a nine-day stay. They did not disclose the nature of his illness.

Analysts said the sharp reaction in Ekran's stock to the rumours was clear evidence of the close identification of Ting to his companies and the Bakun dam. The billionaire's empire includes property, timber processing, construction and a regional airline.

The dam, which will be one of the largest in Asia when it is completed by 2002, is located in the remote interior of Malaysia's Borneo state of Sarawak. Environmentalists managed to halt preliminary work on the dam with a court order in July, which was later overturned.
Minority shareholders of the Bakun company -- Tenaga and Malaysia Mining Corp Bhd -- are reportedly balking at Ekran's demand for more than one billion ringgit in management fees.
Tenaga, under new chairman Ahmad Tajuddin, is said to be seeking more control of the management process. It holds about 25 percent of the dam company.
Tenaga and Malaysia Mining officials declined immediate comment.

Adding to the stew was an unusual statement issued by Ting over the weekend that three newspapers owned by a company affiliated with him were being unfairly blamed for the unexpected defeat of former Sarawak deputy chief minister Wong Soon Kai in state elections earlier this month.
Wong is a close ally of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, who is also an ardent backer of the dam.
In a statement quoted by the national Bernama news agency on Saturday, Ting said: "If the three newspapers' coverage has violated laws, legal action is the most appropriate measure."

Analysts say it is anyone's guess why the Bakun dam contract signing was delayed. But it is undeniable that Ting is the key to the deal. "He's seen as the person who can pull it off without too many hassles," said one Ekran analyst. "It's hard to replace that driving momentum."
